# A Map of AI-for-Architecture Work {#sec-appendix-b-ai-for-architecture-map}

::: {.abstract}
This appendix consolidates the prior body of AI-for-architecture work that Architecture 2.0 builds on. We group established results into families, map each family to the principal life-cycle stages for which the cited work demonstrates activity and to the chapter that develops it, and state how the discipline in this book differs from any single family. The map serves as a reading aid and a positioning statement, not a comprehensive survey.
:::

Machine learning has appeared in computer architecture for decades. Early work proposed learned in-chip mechanisms and models of architecture design spaces. More recent systems couple learned methods to simulators, compilers, and implementation tools. The families below form the foundation our work draws on. We collect them for a narrow purpose. This is not another survey, since existing work already provides that [@ChenPenneyJimenez2020AIArchitecture]. Instead, we offer a positioning aid to show what each family contributes, which principal life-cycle stages the cited work demonstrates, and where we put these methods to use (@tbl-ai-arch-map).

Most method families in the table fall into three regimes, and each regime supports a different claim. Learned in-chip components occupy the mechanism regime and we evaluate them against the mechanism's own budget, such as mispredict rate at fixed storage and latency. Learned cost models occupy the design-space-model regime and we evaluate them based on their predictive fidelity against the tool they approximate. Families that participate in the design process itself occupy the third regime. Benchmarks and datasets sit alongside these regimes as supporting evaluation infrastructure. We take the normative position that a complete third-regime result must be judged at the level of the architecture study, not by the generated artifact alone. Confusing the regimes allows a bounded branch-prediction result to become evidence for trusting an agent with a floorplan, which it clearly is not.

| **Family of work** | **Representative results** | **Principal life-cycle stages demonstrated** | **Developed in** | **Key sources** |
| – | – | – | – | – |
| **Learned in-chip components** | Perceptron branch predictors and learned prefetchers, where learning is embedded in the mechanism itself and does a bounded tactical job | Implement, Evaluate | @sec-moonshot, @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization | [@JimenezLin2001Perceptron; @ChenPenneyJimenez2020AIArchitecture] |
| **Learned cost models and predictive DSE** | Surrogates and regression models that predict performance and power across a design space from cheap features | Explore, Evaluate | @sec-data-representations-world-models, @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization | [@IpekEtAl2006PredictiveDSE; @LeeBrooks2006RegressionModeling; @BaiEtAl2021BOOMExplorer] |

: **The unit of work in Architecture 2.0 is the architecture study and its reviewable claim, not any single family's artifact:** each row names prior results, the principal life-cycle stages demonstrated by the cited work, and the chapters that develop it. The stage column uses only the six labels defined in @sec-architecture-20-ontology. {#tbl-ai-arch-map tbl-colwidths="[20,28,15,22,15]"}

These families are not mutually exclusive. An agentic design-space search might call a learned cost model, invoke an autoscheduler, and emit RTL. This means a single architecture study can touch several rows at once.

The learned in-chip components family carries a filter the others do not. A proposed component is only useful when its inference fits the mechanism's storage and latency budget. The perceptron predictor provides a bounded example, keeping within a 4\ KB hardware budget and delivering a prediction in one cycle [@JimenezLin2001Perceptron]. This result ties predictive accuracy directly to the resources we consume inside the mechanism.

These families also occupy distinct regions of the territory drawn in @fig-book-composition. The learned-components, cost-model, autotuning, and co-design families live where architecture meets ML. Reinforcement learning for physical design and LLM-driven RTL generation live where ML meets EDA. Kahng describes learned models that use earlier-stage features to predict routing hotspots and downstream-flow outcomes [@Kahng2018Machine]. We can view these surrogates as the cost-model family applied to physical design, where a cheap prediction guides our iteration before we run a more expensive downstream flow. Generated assertions and testbenches span both regions, but they remain candidate verification collateral that we must independently execute and review [@FangEtAl2025AssertLLM; @QiuEtAl2024AutoBench; @KangEtAl2024FVEval]. As the corresponding rows in @tbl-ai-arch-map show, AgentDSE places tool feedback inside exploration, while QuArch contributes an Evaluate-stage test of architecture knowledge and question answering.

Reading down the stage column reveals a related asymmetry. Explore appears in five rows, Implement in six, and Evaluate in five. Notably, no row demonstrates Formulate, Interpret and Explain, or Review and Decide. We add those responsibilities to our normative standard for a complete architecture study.

Because we often combine these methods, what separates Architecture 2.0 from any single family is our unit of work. A learned branch predictor changes one mechanism. A macro-placement agent proposes a candidate for one implementation step. An RTL-generating model produces one artifact. We judge each result on that bounded output alone.

Our work instead takes the complete architecture study and its reviewable claim as the unit. The question is not just whether a model produced a plausible artifact, but whether the whole loop, from intent through tools to evidence, supports an architectural decision that another architect can inspect and challenge. The families mapped here supply the methods. Our discipline supplies the standard of judgment that decides what their outputs are actually worth.

## Candidates, Not Decisions

These model outputs are always candidates, never final decisions. An autoscheduler's proposed schedule supports a performance claim only after we measure its execution on the relevant hardware. A proposed placement requires downstream place-and-route, timing, power, and congestion checks. Generated RTL requires rigorous functional and implementation checks. Qualified engineers in the accountable organization retain acceptance responsibility, while verification and implementation owners retain signoff for their respective domains.

Candidates can mislead us through false confidence or hidden total costs. Generated assertions can pass vacuously while checking nothing that actually matters, so their apparent success is not independent evidence [@BeerEtAl2001Vacuity; @Clarke2018ModelChecking] (@sec-feedback-verification-trust). When we assess macro-placement methods such as AlphaChip, a fair total-cost comparison must include the pretraining and fine-tuning runs actually used for the reported design, together with their compute [@ChengEtAl2026UpdatedAssessment]. Neither apparent verification success nor a favorable cost comparison replaces our required acceptance and signoff.
